newsitem.title: CUBA: Peru's Fujimori holds talks with Castro in Havana.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori holds talks with Castro in Havana.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, on a surprise trip to Cuba, held talks with President Fidel Castro on Monday that were expected to include discussions of Peru's hostage crisis.

Fujimori, who flew in from the Dominican Republic, was met at Havana's Jose Marti airport by Castro and other senior government officials. Shortly afterward he began official talks with Castro at the Council of State in Havana.

There was no official word on the agenda for their talks. But resolution of the 76-day-old hostage crisis, in which some 20 Marxist rebels are holding 72 men at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, was believed a major focus.
Government Palace spokesman Israel Mertz told Reuters in Lima that Fujimori's trip to Cuba was a surprise to officials there so they do not know the details of the discussions.

"While its not official, maybe they will talk about the hostage crisis," the spokesman said, adding that Peruvian-Cuban issues and Cuba's relations with the rest of the region would also likely be discussed.
Fujimori flew to Santo Domingo on Sunday afternoon on a quick trip to talk about the crisis in Lima.
His unexpected arrival in Havana capped weeks of speculation that Cuba might be asked to play a role to end Latin America's longest hostage crisis.

But Cuba has declined all comment on such speculation. Cuban government officials on Monday made no immediate comment on the purpose of Fujimori's visit and did not even confirm the Peruvian leader was coming until his plane arrived.

There was no word on how long the talks with Castro would last. However, Foreign Ministry officials said a news conference was scheduled at the Council of State for the early afternoon. However, they gave no other details.
Fujimori had been thought to be returning to Lima on Monday after visiting the Dominican Republic, where he held a 3 1/2 hour meeting on Sunday with President Leonel Fernandez.

Peru-based journalists who travelled on a separate plane to cover Fujimori's trip to the Dominican Republic arrived in Havana just before the Peruvian leader. They said they were completely unaware of where they were going until shortly before arriving in Cuba.
News reports have said Cuba, Nicaragua or a country in Eastern Europe could be potential places of asylum for the rebels.
Peruvian media reported on Monday that the Dominican Republic may take six of the hostage-takers.

While ruling out the main demand of the rebels -- the release of 400 jailed comrades -- Fujimori has indicated he might make other concessions. He has always left the way open to asylum in another country for the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary (MRTA) rebels, who seized their captives on Dec 17.

From the start, Cuba was cited in foreign news reports as a possible mediator in the crisis, or as a place of refuge for the rebels. The MRTA is said to be inspired by Cuba's revolution but it is not known to have any links with Havana.

Castro mediated in June 1995 to secure the freedom of the brother of former Colombian president Cesar Gaviria, kidnapped by a Colombian guerrilla group. Some of the kidnappers and their families flew to Cuba.
Havana also intervened to help resolve a crisis in Colombia in 1980 when guerrillas of the M-19 movement seized 14 ambassadors at the Dominican Embassy residence in Bogota.
That siege lasted two months and ended without bloodshed when the guerrillas dropped their demands and freed their hostages, flying to Cuba in a plane sent by Castro.
The heavily armed squad of mainly teenage MRTA rebels originally took hundreds of hostages but freed many of them in the first weeks, including two Cuban diplomats.
Meanwhile, government officials and guerrilla leaders were slated on Monday to hold an eighth round of face-to-face talks in Lima to find a peaceful end to the hostage crisis.
